result_expr: 6*gamma/eps*phi(x, y, z, t)**2*(1 - phi(x, y, z, t))**2 + 3*gamma*eps/2*(Derivative(phi(x, y, z, t), x)**2 + Derivative(phi(x, y, z, t), y)**2 + Derivative(phi(x, y, z, t), z)**2)

symbols.name: W
symbols.meaning: height coefficient of the double-well (bulk) term; fixed to 6 gamma/eps in S5

symbols.name: kappa
symbols.meaning: gradient-energy coefficient; fixed to 3 gamma eps in S5

symbols.name: X
symbols.meaning: coordinate normal to a flat interface, with X=0 at phi=1/2

symbols.name: ell
symbols.meaning: intrinsic decay length of the equilibrium profile, sqrt(kappa/(2W))

symbols.name: phi_0
symbols.meaning: equilibrium profile across a flat interface

symbols.name: sigma
symbols.meaning: excess free energy per unit area of a flat equilibrium interface

symbols.name: delta
symbols.meaning: interface width, defined as 1 / max |d phi_0/dX| (the distance over which the tangent at the midpoint rises from 0 to 1)

steps.title: Ansatz: double well plus gradient
steps.why: At coexistence the bulk energy must have two equal-depth minima at $\phi=0$ (gas) and $\phi=1$ (ice), so neither phase is favored; $g(\phi)=\phi^2(1-\phi)^2$ is the lowest-order polynomial with this property and a barrier $g(1/2)=1/16$ between them. A gradient term penalizes sharp changes, so the interface gets a finite width and a positive energy; without it the interface would be infinitely sharp.
steps.operation: choose the Ginzburg-Landau form with coefficients W and kappa still free

steps.title: Euler-Lagrange equation for a flat interface
steps.why: Equilibrium means $\delta F/\delta\phi=0$. For a flat interface $\phi$ depends only on the normal coordinate $X$, with $\phi\to0$ as $X\to-\infty$ and $\phi\to1$ as $X\to+\infty$.
steps.operation: take the variational derivative of F and restrict to phi = phi_0(X)

check.printed: EL residual: 0 (for the profile of S3)

steps.title: First integral and profile
steps.why: Multiply S2 by $\phi_0'$ and integrate once; the constant is zero because $\phi_0'\to0$ and $g\to0$ in the bulk. This equipartition gives $\phi_0'=\sqrt{2W/\kappa}\,\phi_0(1-\phi_0)$, solved by a logistic profile with decay length $\ell=\sqrt{\kappa/(2W)}$.
steps.operation: multiply by phi_0', integrate over X, then separate variables

steps.title: Interface energy
steps.why: The excess energy per area is the integral of $f$ across the interface (the bulk value is 0). With equipartition the integrand is $\kappa\phi_0'^2$, and changing variables from $X$ to $\phi$ gives a closed form.
steps.operation: integrate f over X, substitute dX = dphi/phi_0'

check.printed: sigma = sqrt(2)*sqrt(W)*sqrt(kappa)/6; numeric sigma 0.577350269189626 equals formula 0.577350269189626 for W=3, kappa=2

steps.title: Fix the coefficients
steps.why: Require $\sigma=\gamma$ and choose $\ell=\varepsilon/2$, so that the profile is $\phi_0=\tfrac12[1+\tanh(X/\varepsilon)]$. Solving the two equations gives $W$ and $\kappa$ in terms of $\gamma$ and $\varepsilon$.
steps.operation: solve sigma = gamma, ell = eps/2 for W and kappa

steps.title: Width and direct energy check
steps.why: With these coefficients the tanh profile solves S2, and its energy integral is exactly $\gamma$. Defining the width as $\delta=1/\max|\phi_0'|$ gives $\delta=2\varepsilon$; the 10%-90% width is $2\ln 3\,\varepsilon\approx2.20\,\varepsilon$.
steps.operation: substitute S5 into S2 and S4

check.printed: EL residual tanh profile: 0; 1/max slope = 2*epsilon; 10-90 width = 2*epsilon*log(3) = 2.197 eps; sigma direct = gamma

steps.title: Free energy density
steps.why: Substitute S5 into S1. Both terms have units J m$^{-3}$.

check.printed: bulk term: kg m^-1 s^-2; gradient term: kg m^-1 s^-2; same: True

assumptions_used: A1: The temperature is uniform and constant, at phase coexistence (given), so the bulk free energies of ice and gas are equal and the well has two minima of equal depth; the common bulk value is set to zero.
A2: The interface energy $\gamma$ is isotropic, so the gradient coefficient is a scalar constant.
A3: The free energy is local and depends only on $\phi$ and $\nabla\phi$ (square-gradient, Ginzburg-Landau form); the double well is the quartic $\phi^2(1-\phi)^2$.
A4: For calibration we use a flat, one-dimensional interface at equilibrium, far from walls, with $\phi\to0$ and $\phi\to1$ on the two sides.
A5: Width convention: $\delta=1/\max|d\phi_0/dX|=2\varepsilon$, where the profile is $\tfrac12[1+\tanh(X/\varepsilon)]$.

neglected.effect: Driving force for sublimation and deposition (tilting term, for example proportional to $(T-T_m)$ or vapor supersaturation, times $h(\phi)$)
neglected.why: The work order is at coexistence, so this term is zero by assumption A1.

neglected.effect: Anisotropy of the ice surface energy (hexagonal ice facets)
neglected.why: Taken as isotropic (A2). The anisotropy of ice-vapor surface energy is a few percent, which is small compared with the geometric effects of pore confinement.

neglected.effect: Regolith grain surfaces: wetting and the ice-grain and gas-grain energies
neglected.why: The work order treats the pore space as ice plus gas only. Contact angles would enter through boundary terms, not through $f$.

neglected.effect: Coupling to temperature and vapor density fields (latent heat, vapor diffusion)
neglected.why: At constant uniform temperature and coexistence they do not change the equilibrium interface. They belong to the dynamics, not to this functional.

neglected.effect: Elastic strain energy in ice and density change on phase change
neglected.why: Ice in open pores against low-pressure gas is nearly stress-free. Elastic energy in the bulk is much smaller than $\gamma/\varepsilon$ for nanometer-to-micron $\varepsilon$.
Calibration uses a flat interface. Curved interfaces get corrections of relative order $\varepsilon/R$, which are small when $\varepsilon$ is much smaller than the pore radius $R$.
They are excluded by the deliverable. They are of relative order $(\varepsilon/L)^2$ on scales $L\gg\varepsilon$.
